# 1. Project introduction and strategic questions

## 1.1. Business problem

In the Iranian labor market, a job posting does three things at once: it announces the employer's demand, it shows the employer's expectation level for skills and experience, and, when salary is declared, it reveals the offered price of labor. Aggregated over time, these postings build a quantitative picture of “who hires whom, with what skills, where and at what price”.

JobVision, as one of Iran's largest job platforms, has published its posting data publicly. This data offers a rare opportunity for labor market analysis, but it is raw: 43 columns of different types, free Persian text, JSON structures, missing values and one fundamental limitation — only about one third of postings declare salary.

The goal of this project is to turn this raw data into **actionable insight** for three audiences:

- **HR manager or business owner:** With what salary and benefits should we hire? When and under what conditions should we publish the posting? Which skill really adds value?
- **Job seeker:** Which skill, degree, experience and geography yields the highest financial return? How large is the gender and provincial gap?
- **Policymaker and labor market analyst:** In which seasons does demand peak? Which sectors are growing or shrinking? How has geographic concentration changed?

## 1.2. Our role in this project

We act as JobVision's data analysis team. The CEO and HR manager of a fictional company, “Robehrashd”, have asked us to deliver a documented picture of the market before drafting next year's hiring plan. So every analysis must be tied to one of these decisions: **whom should we hire, at what price, at what time and under what conditions?**

## 1.3. Four management questions

The project brief raises four high-level questions. These questions are broken down into measurable indicators so that the answers can be checked and rejected or confirmed.

**Table 1.1 | Map of management questions, indicators and answering sections**

| Management question | Indicator and basis of measurement | Answering sections |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What is a competitive compensation package for each job level and province? | Median and quartiles of monthly salary and hourly income by job category, province, experience and degree | 7, 10, 12, 13, 14, 22 |
| In which season does demand peak, and which skills carry financial added value? | Monthly and Shamsi time series, seasonal index, price premium of skills, growth in skill demand | 10, 19, 22 |
| What is the structure of employer competition, and how does a posting become distinctive? | Salary disclosure rate, provincial and industry concentration, employer typology, differentiating benefits | 9, 14, 20, 22 |
| What capacities does the data have for creating value for stakeholders? | Combining the findings into a proposal package and a decision dashboard | 22, 23 |

**Note on table 1.1:** this table is not itself an analysis result; it is a roadmap. Each indicator has a defined unit, sample and period and is defined separately in its own section. For example, “median salary” is computed only on postings that declare salary, whereas the “salary disclosure rate” is measured on all postings; the two cannot be read in place of each other.

## 1.4. Analysis approach

The path from raw data to decision has five steps:

1. **Profiling and quality control:** size, types, missingness, duplication, range and cardinality. Without this step, every later number may be meaningless.
2. **Building the analysis layer:** we build a single posting-level table in which all numeric, categorical and textual features are extracted. Auxiliary tables for skills, education and benefits are also built once and reused across all sections so that computation is not repeated.
3. **Exploratory and statistical analysis:** distribution, correlation, hypothesis testing and analysis of the missingness mechanism.
4. **Modeling and unsupervised learning:** salary regression to identify determinants, clustering of job titles and the skills network.
5. **Translation into decisions:** the compensation package table, the posting calendar and the posting text checklist.

## 1.5. A few basic terms

- **Job posting:** one data row. Its identifier is `ad_id`. One company can have several postings; therefore counting postings is not the same as counting companies.
- **Salary disclosure:** `Jobpost_SalaryCanBeShown == True` means the posting declared the salary range. Otherwise the salary value is empty, not zero.
- **Monthly salary:** the midpoint of the declared salary range, in units of **million tomans per month**. This number is not the contract amount; it is the price offered in the posting.
- **Hourly income:** monthly salary divided by monthly working hours estimated from the “working hours” text. This indicator is needed to compare full-time, part-time and project-based jobs, because monthly salary alone does not show working hours.
- **Job category:** `Jobpost_MainJobCategory`, the main specialization of the posting (for example “Software development and programming”). **Industry:** `Jobpost_IndustryFa`, the employer's field of activity (for example “Information technology / software and hardware”). The two are not the same: an industrial company can hire a programmer.
- **Gender preference:** the text of the posting, not the gender of the person hired. “Men only” means the employer made hiring a man a requirement.
- **Age range:** the minimum and maximum age requested by the employer, not the actual age of job seekers.
- **Outlier:** a value far from the body of the distribution. We do not remove outliers; we flag them, keep them in the description and restrict them only in modeling, using a transparent rule.

## 1.6. From number to insight

In this notebook every claim has three components: **number**, **comparison** and **limitation**. For example, “the median salary of the information technology category is 14.5 million tomans and 38% above the median of the whole market” is an insight; the number 14.5 on its own is not information. At the end of each section, the “Answer” and “Business summary” sentences follow the same structure.

> **Golden rule:** we never report an indicator without its denominator and sample. Wherever the sample is small we give a warning; wherever the difference is not significant we say so.

## 2.4. What is not in the data

Attention to the “absences” matters as much as attention to the “presences”:

- **The full posting text and job description** are not present; only the title, skills, benefits and hiring requirements.
- **Company name** has been anonymized; competition analysis is done at the level of company attributes, not brand.
- **The exact publication date** is not present; only the month.
- **Job seeker information, successful hires, actual contract salaries and retention rates** are not present.
- **Inflation adjustment** is not in the data; values are nominal and time comparisons must be interpreted with an inflation index.
- **Hourly wage** is not recorded directly; it must be derived from monthly salary and working hours.

## 2.5. Salary unit: why million tomans?

The data card states the salary unit as “Toman”, but the range of values (2 to 100 with a median of 10) is not consistent with raw “toman”: a monthly salary of 10 tomans is meaningless. Three pieces of evidence show that the real scale is **million tomans per month**:

1. The median of the declared minimum salary is 10 and the median maximum is 12; this is consistent with the market wage level in 1401–1402.
2. The 99th percentile of the minimum salary is 35 and the maximum is 70; a range that is reasonable for managers and specialized roles in those years.
3. If the scale were “thousand tomans”, a median of 10 thousand tomans per month would not be consistent with any standard.

This assumption is applied uniformly throughout the notebook. If the data scale changes, all salary numbers must be recomputed.

## 2.7. Ethical considerations and license

The data is public and anonymous, but it carries three ethical considerations: (1) analysis of gender and age can help reproduce discrimination; we carry it out to **identify gaps**, not to prescribe discrimination. (2) Postings are employer preferences and are not attributed to actual workers. (3) The CC BY-NC 4.0 license does not permit commercial use and the source must be cited.

**Reading tables 6.1 and 6.2:** the market aggregates into three wage layers: 16.8% of postings below 8 million, 71.9% between 8 and 20 million and 11.3% above 20 million tomans. The middle layer is the body of the administrative, sales and services labor market; the layer above 20 million, which accounts for less than one ninth of postings, belongs to specialized, engineering and managerial roles.

The type of declared range also reveals a managerial pattern: no posting declared a range narrower than 15%; that is, Iranian employers almost always build a negotiation margin of at least 15 percent into the posting. # 7. Analyzing distributions, skewness, and outliers

The question of this section is simple: what shape do the key variables have? The answer determines whether we use the median or the mean, and which values are outliers.

## 7.1. Statistical summary of numeric variables

## 7.4. How much can we trust the medians? Confidence intervals via bootstrap resampling

All the numbers in this project come from a sample of job postings, so every median is an **estimate**, not a definite fact. For this reason, we estimate the 95% confidence interval of the medians using bootstrap resampling (bootstrap, 400 repetitions): job postings are resampled with replacement, and the spread of the median across these samples shows the uncertainty. A narrow number means “this number can be attributed to the market”.

**Interpretation of table 7.5:** The result of the bootstrap resampling is itself a finding, not just a technical check.

- **The monthly median salary has a confidence interval width of zero**: in all 400 resamplings, the median stayed exactly 11.0 million. The reason is what we saw in section 9.4: the market has anchored numbers, and the median sits on the anchors. That means this number can be confidently attributed to the whole market.
- **The mean is the only index with a non-zero confidence interval**: 13.34 to 13.43 million (width 0.08). Because the right tail extends to 85 million, the mean is sensitive to a few expensive postings; this is the technical reason why the reports throughout this project are based on the **median**.
- **The disclosure rate and the share of postings above 15 million** (26.7%, bounds 26.5 to 27.0) have an interval of less than half a unit — meaning these ratios can be attributed to the whole market.
- At the category level, **the median hourly income of professional sales has the widest interval** (70.8 to 74.2, width 3.4) because the roles within this category are very diverse; in contrast, finance and accounting is more compact with a width of 1.4.

**Practical implication:** The main uncertainty in this project does not come from “data dispersion” but from the **sample size of the groups** (section 9.4). So wherever a group's sample is small, caution is needed; the medians themselves do not need a margin of error.

## 8.4. Scatter and comparison figures: the relationship at the posting level

The correlation matrix tells the direction and strength of the relationship, but it hides three things: the shape of the relationship, the dispersion within each level, and the points that break the pattern. This subsection shows these with three views:

1. **Weekly hours × hourly income** — the mechanics of the hourly index: the more hours, the larger the denominator and the lower the hourly income.
2. **Experience × monthly salary** with a median line and an interquartile range band — an upward relationship with diminishing returns in a single view.
3. **Number of benefits × salary** as a box plot — comparing distributions, not just the median.

For readability, in the scatter plots a sample of 9,000 postings (from `hourly_ready`) is plotted with low opacity, and the median line is computed on the entire original data.

**Interpretation of tables 8.4 and 8.5 and figure 8.5:** The three views show three different things.

# 9. The mechanism of salary missingness: random or dependent?

Three-quarters of postings do not disclose salary. The key question is whether this concealment is related to observable characteristics (company size, province, job category, type of cooperation) or not. If the missingness is dependent and structured, it has two important consequences: first, the salary analysis is biased toward a particular segment of the market; second, “disclosure or non-disclosure” itself becomes a studyable employer behavior.

## 9.1. Disclosure rate across different dimensions
86:
**Interpretation of tables 9.1 to 9.4:** Salary missingness is highly structured. The disclosure rate is inversely related to company size: companies with 11 to 50 employees publish 43.4% of their postings with salary, while companies with 1001 to 5000 employees publish only 16.6%. This difference of 26.8 percentage points is the largest gap across all dimensions: a small company uses transparency as a competitive tool to attract people in an unknown market, while a large company relies on brand and career path.

Job category also has a clear pattern: postings for general laborers (47.8%), salespeople and medical reps (44.6%), and digital marketing (42.3%) are the most transparent, while DevOps and technical support (18.2%) and programming (24.9%) have the least transparency. That is, the more knowledge-based the role and the higher the salary, the less public disclosure.

Remote work makes the biggest difference for a binary characteristic: 52.5% of remote work postings disclose salary, versus 31.6% of on-site postings. A remote work posting competes with the global market, and salary transparency becomes more essential for it. Provinces do not show a big difference (30.7% in Alborz to 39.5% in East Azerbaijan); therefore “geography” alone is not explanatory.
87: ## 9.2. Significance test: chi-square and Cramér's effect size
89:
**Interpretation of table 9.5:** All chi-square tests are significant at the 0.001 level, meaning the assumption of “missing completely at random (MCAR)” is rejected. But statistical significance is not the same as effect size: the largest Cramér's V belongs to company size (0.188) and job category (0.147), which falls in the “weak to moderate” range; remote work (0.112) and internship (0.094) follow, and the other dimensions are below 0.1. That is, the dependency is real, but none of these characteristics alone determines the disclosure rate.

A methodological note: with a sample of 360 thousand, even small differences become significant; that is why reporting effect size alongside the p-value is essential.
90: ## 9.3. Logistic regression model for the probability of salary disclosure
92:
**Interpretation of tables 9.6 and 9.7 and the final answer:** The logistic regression model shows that the odds of salary disclosure for general laborer postings is 2.76 times the baseline level, for remote work postings 2.36 times, and for salesperson/medical rep 2.33 times; in contrast, part-time postings have lower odds (0.65) of disclosure. All these coefficients are statistically significant, but the model's performance is limited: McFadden's pseudo-R2 is 0.05 and the area under the ROC curve is 0.65, and the classification accuracy (68.1%) is only 1.2 percentage points better than the baseline model (always “not disclosed”).

**Answer to the project question:** Salary missingness is **not missing completely at random (MCAR)**; it depends on observable variables — especially company size, job category, and remote work. Therefore the missingness model is of the **MAR** type (dependent on the observed data). But the explained share is small; that is, a large part of the disclosure decision is each employer's internal policy and unobservable characteristics.

**Practical implication:** The salary means and medians in this data are biased toward small companies, administrative/sales/service roles, and remote and contract postings. For specialized roles and large companies, these numbers indicate the market floor, not the actual level of competition. In section 22 this limitation is taken into account in the salary recommendations.

The project brief has two explicit requirements in this very section: first, the **frequency of available salary values** should be analyzed — because all wage analyses stand on these numbers, and their shape determines which statistic is valid; second, any group in which **the number of postings with disclosed salary is close to zero** should be reported, so the reader knows which result is built on a small sample and should not be generalized to the whole market.

In this subsection we first see what numbers employers actually write (not just the median and quartiles), and then we list the small-sample groups across four key dimensions.

**Interpretation of table 9.8 and figure 9.1:** The most important finding of this subsection is the extreme discreteness of salaries: 119,048 postings with salary have only **40 unique values**. The five most frequent values — **13.5** (21.3%), **9.0** (19.1%), **11.0** (16.0%), **17.5** (15.4%), and **7.0** (11.5%) — together make up **83.4%** of postings, and the first ten values **99.1%**. In other words, the Iranian employer announces salary as a “band”, not a continuous value.

The composition of the numbers is also meaningful: 51.7% are integers and 48.3% end in “point five”. Figure 9.1-b shows that this pattern changes with the salary level — below 8 million, 68% are integers; in the 8 to 11 million range, **100%** (that is, there is no half-unit number in this range); and above 15 million, only 18.8% (because 17.5 and 22.5 dominate). Three methodological consequences: (1) the median and quartiles are fully meaningful, because they sit on these very anchors; (2) drawing a continuous “density” on this data is misleading — that is why in section 7 a histogram with bins was chosen, not KDE; (3) in the models we used `log_salary` so that the right skew is tamed and this discreteness does not have a damaging effect.

# 10. Time trend, seasonality and wage dynamics

## 10.1. Job posting volume over time
101:
**Interpretation of Table 10.1 and Figure 10.1:** job posting volume rose from 12,782 in Farvardin 1401 to 24,017 in Mehr 1402; nearly 88% growth over 19 months. The trend is not uniform: Esfand 1401, with 5,531 postings, is the trough of the period, and Farvardin 1402, with a 229% jump relative to it, shows that this decline was mostly seasonal and temporary. The three-month moving average also confirms the long-term rise.

The Bahman and Esfand drop and the Farvardin surge are a familiar pattern of the Iranian job market: employers stop hiring before the Nowruz holidays and, immediately afterwards, the accumulated postings are published.
102: ## 10.2. Seasonality with the Solar Hijri calendar
104:
**Interpretation of Tables 10.2 and 10.3 and Figure 10.2:** the seasonal index shows a clear peak in **Dey** (123%) and then **Mehr and Aban** (115 and 112%); the lowest months are **Bahman** (79%), **Khordad** (86%) and **Shahrivar** (88%). In other words, the job market is more active in the second half of the year and before the end of the Solar Hijri year, and it quietens down on the eve of Nowruz and during the summer holidays.

We deliberately excluded Esfand from the seasonal index: Esfand 1401 had only 5,531 postings and Esfand 1402 is incomplete in the data; had we included it, the index would have become a misleading figure (18%) because of a single observation.

**Methodological caveat:** because the total market volume grew over these two years, the closing months of each year naturally have more postings. The seasonal index does not fully remove the growth trend; so read it as the “direction of the seasonal pattern”, not as a precise forecasting coefficient.

107:
**Interpretation of Tables 10.4 to 10.6 and Figure 10.3:** the median salary rose from 7 million tomans in Farvardin 1401 to 13.5 million in Bahman 1402; comparing like-named months, nominal growth is **53.7%**. ## 10.5. In which groups and industries does the seasonal jump occur?

The seasonal index in Section 10.2 was for the whole market. The project brief asks more explicitly: at **what times and in which groups and industries** do these jumps occur? If all categories rise at the same time, the seasonal peak is a “general market wave”; if the categories follow different patterns, the peak has its own date for each employer — and that difference translates directly into the hiring calendar.

Method: the same restriction as Section 10.2 (excluding Esfand, because one year of it is incomplete) and the same index definition — the number of postings in each month divided by the monthly mean of that same group × 100, so comparisons between small and large groups are valid.
114:
**Interpretation of Tables 10.8 and 10.9 and Figure 10.5:** the overall picture is that the market's seasonal peak is **not a single general wave**; 9 job categories out of 11 peak in **Dey**, but the intensity and the minimum months differ, and two categories follow a completely separate pattern.

- **Software development** has the sharpest seasonality: a Dey index of **147.7** against **75.5** in Shahrivar — a range of 72 units. This is the pattern seen in the technology job market: budget approvals and project starts in Dey, and a hiring slump in the summer and Shahrivar.
- **Digital marketing and SEO** peaks in **Farvardin** (**132.7**) and its minimum is **Bahman**. The reason is clear: the fiscal year for advertising and campaigns starts with Farvardin.
- **General labourer and service worker** peaks in **Aban** (**122.5**), not Dey — this category is tied to the working season and seasonal projects (construction, warehousing, end-of-year sales).
- **Finance and accounting** is the least volatile category (range of 42 units); because these roles are needed in every month and are not tied to a project.

At the industry level, two exceptions also appear: **pharmaceuticals** with a peak in **Mehr** (**136.9**) — coinciding with the reopening of schools and the cold season — and **fast-moving consumer goods** with a Mehr peak (**117.1**). The rest of the industries, including internet (**135**) and information technology (**134.4**), peak in Dey; that is, the technology industry not only has the largest volume, it also produces the largest seasonal peak.

**Practical implication for the employer:** the “best time to publish a posting” is not the same for everyone. A software company that posts in Shahrivar is publishing in its own lowest month of the year and must raise the salary range to compensate; whereas a digital marketing team must not miss Farvardin. This table is a direct input to the hiring calendar in Section 22.

**Methodological caveat:** the same restriction from Section 10.2 holds — because the total market volume grew over these two years, the closing months of the year naturally have more postings. But because all groups are normalised by the same definition (their own monthly mean = 100), comparisons across groups are valid, even if the “absolute value” of the index is subject to the trend.

**Interpretive warning:** the data record the employer's preference in the posting text, not the gender of the person hired and not individual salaries. ## 12.1. Returns to degree
130:
**Interpretation of Tables 12.1 and 12.2:** in postings that disclose a salary, 61.6% do not state a degree level. Among the rest, bachelor's dominates with 30.9%, and master's and PhD together only 3.1%. 131: ## 12.2. Regression model for a direct comparison of degree and experience
133:
**Interpretation of Tables 12.3 and 12.4:** in the regression model controlling for job category, province and company size, each year of experience adds **+11.1%** and each step of degree (bachelor's → master's) **+14.9%** to salary. **Practical conclusion:** one step of degree is worth roughly **1.3 years of experience**. If an employer is choosing between “a bachelor's with 3 years of experience” and “a master's with 1.7 years of experience”, they are roughly equivalent in terms of market pay.
134: ## 12.3. Where Does Experience Take the Place of a Degree?
136:
**Interpretation of table 12.5 and figures 12.1 and 12.2:** The returns to degree and to work experience are not the same and depend on the industry:

- In **information technology**, the returns to both degree and work experience are about +30% (ratio 1.0); that is, degree and experience are equivalent.
- In **manufacturing and trade**, the return to work experience (+50%) is greater than the return to degree (+29.6%) (ratio 1.7).
- In **internet and e-commerce**, the return to work experience reaches **+94%** and degree +29.6%; that is, experience practically takes the place of a degree (ratio 3.2).
- In **engineering services and automotive**, the return to degree is zero and the return to work experience is positive; in these industries a degree is almost worthless.

Overall pattern: in knowledge-based and mature industries, degree and work experience are equivalent; in fast-growing industries (internet) and traditional industries (manufacturing, automotive, engineering), experience is worth more.

## 12.5. Returns to Work Experience and Degree Across Salary Deciles

# 16. Salary modelling and shifting feature importance over time

## 16.1. Model design

The goal is to predict the **log of the median salary range** from job, skill, location and organisational features. We take the logarithm because the salary distribution is skewed (Section 7). The base model is ridge regression with standardised features, so that coefficients are comparable across variables. We train a separate model for each year to see how the determining factors have changed over time.

**Methodological controls:** Salary outliers are winsorised at the 1st and 99th percentiles, numeric variables are standardised, categorical variables enter via One-Hot (dropping the first level), and evaluation is done with 5-fold cross-validation.
169: **Interpreting the model design:** The model is trained on 119,048 postings that have a salary; 13 numeric features and 9 categorical features (which One-Hot turns into dozens of columns). Outliers have been winsorised at the 1st and 99th percentiles (5.5 to 40 million tomans) so that a single 85-million posting cannot shift the coefficients. The target variable is the log of salary, so that the skewed distribution is handled.
172:
**Interpreting Table 16.1:** The ridge model has a validation coefficient of determination of **0.44** in both years; that is, about 44% of the variation in log salary is explained by the observed features. The model's mean absolute error is about 2.5 million tomans in 1401 and about 3.4 million tomans in 1402, while the baseline model (predicting the median for everyone) has an error of 3.2 and 4.4 million; the model therefore reduces the error by about 22%.

The gradient-boosted tree model (HistGradientBoosting) reaches an R2 of about 0.58; that is, non-linear relations and interactions add about 14 percentage points of explanatory power. The remaining 42% is the share of factors that are not in the data: company brand, negotiation terms, soft skills, and within-job differences.
173: ## 16.3. Which factors have the largest effect, and how have they changed?
175:
**Interpreting Tables 16.2 and 16.3 and Figures 16.1 and 16.2:** The most important numeric factor in both years is **work experience**: one more standard deviation of experience raises salary by about **+16.1%** in 1401 and about **+12.5%** in 1402. After that come the number of benefits (+4.5 to +2.9), having a field of study (+4.1 to +2.8) and company size (+3.3 to +2.7). Note that **all of these effects became smaller from 1401 to 1402**; that is, in the second year the market gave a smaller reward for the same features.

On the categorical side, the gaps are large and deepening: relative to the reference role (programming), postings for general labourer were about **−55.9%** in 1401 and **−60%** in 1402, administrative clerk **−50.3% to −56.1%** and technical technician **−36.3% to −37.4%**. By contrast, managerial roles in 1402 were about **+28.2%** above the reference.

**Summary:** In a year of high inflation, the returns to individual features (experience, degree, benefits) declined somewhat, but the gap between “types of job” deepened; that is, the fate of a wage has come to depend more than ever on the choice of career path, not on accumulating experience.

## 16.4. Do the signs of the coefficients match theoretical expectation?

The project brief asks one explicit question: “Do the signs of the coefficients match your expectation?” Tables 16.2 and 16.3 showed the magnitude of the effect; here we assess only the **direction**, because it is the direction that confirms or rejects the economic theory of the labour market. For each numeric variable, the prior expectation (recorded before seeing the result) is entered and compared with the estimated sign in both years.
178:
**Interpreting Table 16.4 and Key Numbers 16.3:** Of the 11 variables that had a definite theoretical expectation, **6 variables matched expectation in both years**, 2 variables in only one year, and **3 variables were contrary**. The overall pattern confirms human capital theory:

- **Experience** has the largest effect (**+16.1%** in 1401 and **+12.5%** in 1402) and its sign is correct; but the strength of its reward fell by **22 percent** in the second year.
- **Benefits** (+4.5 → +2.9), **field of study** (+4.1 → +2.8) and **company size** (+3.3 → +2.7) also match and all became smaller. That is, in 1402 the market paid **less** for the same features — exactly what was compared with inflation in Section 10.3.
- **Internship** is negative and worsening (−0.6 → −1.5): an internship really is cheaper and this gap has grown.

There are also three contradictions that are **not bugs but findings**:

1. **`skill_count` is negative** (−1.0 and −0.7) although the expectation was “more skills ⇒ higher salary”. The reason: in this model **job category is controlled for**; within a category, a posting that asks for more skills is usually a more general, lower-paid role. The skill premium should be looked at at the level of “which skill”, not “how many skills” — and that is exactly what Section 22.4 (the salary premium of each skill) does.
2. **`weekly_hours` is negative** (−0.3 and −0.2). This is consistent with the finding in Section 8.4: postings with long hours offer lower monthly salaries. The Iranian market does not pay more money for “more hours”.
3. **`company_age_rank` is negative** (−0.6 and −1.0): older companies (usually manufacturing and family-owned) pay less than young startups.

Two variables (`local_priority` and `is_remote`) changed sign between the two years; that is, they are within the zone of indifference and **no policy should be built on them** — policymaking on an effect that reverses the next year is dangerous.

# 17. Clustering job titles by skills and education

Question: which job titles are close to one another in terms of their “skill and education basket”? To answer, we turn each job title into a vector: the share of that title's postings that request each skill, together with the share of postings requiring a master's degree or higher. We then cluster the titles.
181: **Interpreting the clustering data:** 762 job titles with at least 50 postings were selected, covering 70.7% of postings overall (254,451 postings). The vector of each title has 42 dimensions: the share of 40 frequent skills, the share of master's degrees and median experience. Before clustering, the skill vector is weighted with **TF-IDF** so that ubiquitous skills (Excel and Word) do not take over the whole space — without this step, all titles would fall into one giant cluster.
184: **Interpreting Table 17.1 and Figures 17.1 and 17.2:** The silhouette criterion selects **k=3** with a score of 0.510. The two-dimensional map shows that the space has one large “general mass” and two “specialist islands”; not several clusters of equal size. This is itself a finding: at the skill level, Iran's market of job titles does not have high cluster diversity, and a large part of the roles is run with one shared skill basket (office software + administrative communication).
187:
**Interpreting Table 17.2 and Figure 17.3:** The three clusters are three different worlds:

- **Cluster 1 (642 titles, 233,638 postings, 91.8%):** the general mass of the market — sales, accounting, administration, services. The dominant skill basket: Excel, Word, PowerPoint; median salary 11 million, experience 2 years and a share of master's degrees of only 2%.
- **Cluster 2 (107 titles, 19,413 postings):** senior **finance and accounting** roles — senior accountant, finance manager, head of accounting. Median salary 17.5 million, experience 5 years and 15.4% requiring a master's or higher.
- **Cluster 3 (13 titles, 1,400 postings):** **technical/regulatory** roles — technical officer, regulatory affairs specialist, insurance agency. Median salary 17.5 million and 53.5% requiring a master's or higher.

Managerial message: the main difference between the clusters is not in “software skill”, it is in **seniority level and degree**. To promote a role from cluster 1 to cluster 2, adding one new skill is not enough; the combination of experience and degree is what decides.
188: ## 17.3. Have the cluster boundaries changed over the two years?
190:
**Interpreting Tables 17.3 and 17.4:** Clustering each year independently and matching them gives an adjusted Rand index of **0.952**; that is, the cluster boundaries stayed almost identical across the two years and **no title** moved between equivalent clusters. Table 17.4 also shows that the matching matrix is almost diagonal.

**Conclusion:** Over the two-year window, the “boundaries between jobs” did not change. New skills (WordPress, Google Analytics) moved around within those same clusters, but they did not cause the clusters to merge or split. This is consistent with the finding in Section 19: the skill basket of a title stays fixed and change is gradual.
191: **Signature of each cluster:** Table 17.2 gave the full profile of the clusters. The project brief explicitly asks “what differences they have from one another and which titles are in each cluster”. For a compact answer, for each cluster we show the skills that have the **largest distance from the overall mean** — that is, exactly what sets the cluster apart from the rest, not the things that are common to all clusters.

**Interpreting Table 17.5:** The three clusters are three distinct markets:

- **Cluster 1 — the general body of the market** (642 titles, 233,638 postings, only 2% with a master's degree): the highest-volume part of the market. Core titles “sales specialist, accountant, accounting specialist” and its distinctive skill is graphics and web (+0.6 units), while Excel in it is **2.2 units below** the mean. This cluster is where software skill is in little demand and the roles are general.
- **Cluster 2 — senior finance and accounting** (107 titles, 19,413 postings, median experience 5 years, 15% master's): its signature is Excel (**+13.5 units**) and Word (**+9.2 units**); core titles “senior accountant, finance manager, head of accounting”. - **Cluster 3 — technical-regulatory roles** (13 titles, 1,400 postings, **53.5% master's degrees**): the smallest cluster but the most degree-driven part of the whole market (technical officer, regulatory affairs specialist, insurance sales agency). Here a master's degree is effectively an entry requirement, not an advantage.

**Clustering summary:** The main boundary of the market is “general versus specialised”, not “technical versus non-technical”. The specialised cluster has a small volume (0.5% of postings) but imposes the hardest entry conditions; the finance cluster is experience-driven; and the general cluster is the biggest market for mass recruitment. These three want three different hiring strategies.
194: **Cluster stability with bootstrap resampling:** Clustering was performed once on the data; the right question is whether the clusters hold if we reshuffle 20% of the titles, or whether something different emerges each time. Each time, the ARI (Adjusted Rand Index) metric compares the bootstrap clustering with the baseline clustering; above 0.7 means a stable structure.

**Interpretation of Table 17.6:** The mean ARI over 25 bootstrap resamples (80% of titles each time) is **0.896** — that is, the clustering is stable and the three-part structure interpreted in Sections 17.2 and 17.5 is not random. The cause is clear: the third cluster has only 13 titles. With the random removal of 20% of titles, two or three titles may drop out of this cluster and the boundaries shift. By contrast, the two large clusters (642 and 107 titles) remained stable in all iterations.

**Verdict:** The interpretations concerning the “general market core” and “senior finance” are reliable and generalizable; the interpretation of the small technical-regulatory cluster is directional and is not reported as a definitive fact.

# 20. Profiling and clustering of employers [bonus]

Since company names are anonymized, we describe the employer by observable features: size, age, ownership, scope of activity, industry, province, number of benefits, and posting behavior (salary disclosure, remote work). The data is mixed; therefore we use the **Gower distance**, which combines both numeric and categorical variables into a single distance measure, and then hierarchical clustering is performed on the same distance matrix.

**Interpretation of Tables 20.1 to 20.3 and Figures 20.1 and 20.2:** The Gower distance over a sample of 4,000 job postings shows a clear structure: **two large types** and **two small, distinct types**.

- **Type 3 (24.1%):** Small employers with 1 benefit, disclosure of 39%, and remote work of 10.4% — the “flexible small employer”.

## 20.5. The structure of competition: where is competition intense and where does a posting stand out?

The third question of the project’s outlook was: “What is the structure of competition among employers, and what can a business do to differentiate its job postings?”. The data anonymizes the employer’s name, so we measure competition at the **market** level, not the company level. Four indicators suffice:

- **Posting volume and share**: the more, the greater the competition for attraction.
- **Annual growth**: a market that grows quickly has more future competition.
- **Coefficient of variation of salary** (standard deviation ÷ mean): the higher it is, the less standardized the pricing, and the more room there is for bargaining and differentiation.
- **Disclosure rate**: a low-transparency market is a field for postings that stand out through transparency.
224:
**Interpretation of Table 20.5 and Key Numbers 20.3:** The competitive structure of Iran’s labor market is **not concentrated but is unbalanced**; the concentration index (HHI) is **1852 out of 10,000**, which is a long way from the threshold of 2500 (a concentrated market). That is, no single category holds the field of competition by itself, and competition is spread across all fronts.

- **Where is competition just now flaring up?** Digital marketing with growth of **+153.6%**, general laborer (+78.3%), salesperson and van sales rep (+76.3%), and office clerk (+70.5%) are the fastest-growing arms. Against them, **software development has grown only +6.4%** — that is, this very market, which has the greatest visibility, is in fact the **most mature and most saturated** segment, and competition for attracting staff in it is less dynamic.
- **Where is there more bargaining?** The coefficient of variation of salary is highest in **professional sales and marketing at 58.9%**, then software (52.8%) and finance (50.2%); that is, the market does not agree on the price of these roles, and a posting that states the salary transparently gains the most from differentiation in precisely these categories. By contrast, general laborer (28.6%) and office clerk (32.9%) are the least dispersed — the price of these roles is practically standardized and close to the minimum wage.
- **Where is transparency low?** Network/DevOps (**18%**), industrial engineering (23%), and software (25%) are the least transparent high-volume categories, while general laborer (**47.8%**) and salesperson (44.6%) are the most transparent. The pattern is clear: the more knowledge-intensive the role, the more likely salaries are hidden — and this is **the biggest opportunity for differentiation**.
- **Remote work is elsewhere:** Digital marketing (24.5%) and software (21.5%) have the highest remote-work rates; finance and accounting are practically zero (0.6%).

**An operational answer to the question “how do we differentiate our posting?” — four rules documented from this very data:**

1. **In low-transparency categories, disclose the salary.** In network/DevOps, where only 18% of competitors include a salary, stating a range immediately sets you apart from 82% of the market and — based on Section 9 — transparency in the market for mid-level roles is the main channel of attraction.
2. **For high-variance roles, give a range, not a number.** In professional sales with a coefficient of variation of 59%, a fixed number drives away half the applicants; a range close to the median of that category is both transparent and realistic.
3. **For standard roles, compete on speed and conditions, not salary.** For general laborers and office clerks, the price is nearly fixed; non-cash benefits and the timing of publication (Section 10.5) are the real levers.
4. **Take timing seriously.** Publishing in Dey for technology and finance, in Farvardin for digital marketing, and in Aban for service roles increases the chance of being seen; publishing in Bahman — the lowest month for all categories — lowers that chance.

## 10.6. Monthly demand forecast and its validation

A 23-month series is short, so any forecast on it must be **validated** — otherwise it is a curve, not an estimate. The method has three steps:

1. Hold out the last six months and train the model on the first 17 (SARIMA on the log of volume).
2. Measure the forecast error with the mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) and compare it with a **simple baseline** (the same month one year earlier). If the model is no better than that baseline, it does not deserve to be published.
3. If it wins, refit on all 23 months and forecast the next six months with a confidence interval.

The six-month forecast shows **continued growth**: from 20,656 postings in Esfand 1402 to 25,750 in Mordad 1403 — about **25% above the average of the last three months** in the data. The 80% band is wide (for Mordad 1403, 17,892 to 37,059), which is natural: with 23 monthly points, forecast uncertainty is high.

## 19.5. The words inside a job title: what is each word worth?

Job titles in Iran are built from a handful of recurring words: specialist, manager, operator, officer, assistant… Separating those words lets us estimate **what salary level each one signals** — without a model. This is a simple version of title topic mining: instead of character-level TF-IDF it uses real tokens, because the Persian zero-width non-joiner breaks word boundaries and character n-grams produce unreadable output.
215:
**Reading table 19.5, figure 19.4 and key numbers 19.3:** the words inside a title reveal the salary level better than the title itself, and the pattern is sharp:

- **Seniority words carry the top band:** “Senior” (median 22.5), “Manager,” “Senior,” “Supervisor” and “Head” (17.5 million toman) — between **59% and 105%** above the overall market median of 11 million toman.
- **Role words sit in the middle band:** “Accounting,” “Sales rep,” “Marketing” and “HR” at 13.5 million — about 23% above the market median of 11 million toman.
- **English tokens earn the same premium as their Persian equivalents:** Back, Front, Developer and Specialist are also at 17.5 million; bilingual titling in the tech market does not change the salary band — the difference is categorical, not linguistic.
- **The lowest band appears in support and export-sales words** (13.5 million for terms associated with foreign sales).

**Method note:** 105 words appear in at least 1,500 postings and the table shows 18 of them. This analysis is descriptive and does not control for overlap between words (a title such as “Accounting Manager” contains both); the controlled share of each word is measured in section 19.4, where skill effects are estimated in a model. The practical message is the same for candidates and employers: **one step up in seniority in the title is worth as much as several years of experience.**
